outcome: Angeltveit and McKay proved R(5,5) ≤ 46 (down from the previous best upper bound of 48, which they themselves established in 2017), narrowing the known range from 43 ≤ R(5,5) ≤ 48 to 43 ≤ R(5,5) ≤ 46. The exact value of R(5,5) remains unknown.
summary: The decisive event for this bullet is Angeltveit and McKay's arXiv preprint 'R(5,5) ≤ 46' (arXiv:2409.15709, submitted 2024-09-24, v2 2025-09-01), which improves the upper bound on R(5,5) from 48 (the same authors, 2017) to 46, via 'a combination of linear programming and checking a large number of cases by computer' — no AI system of any kind is mentioned, and the WebFetch of the abstract/paper confirmed no ML, neural network, or SAT-solver framing; this is classical computational combinatorics (LP + exhaustive case-checking, independently re-implemented by both authors as a cross-check). The result was subsequently published in the Journal of Graph Theory 112 (2026): 198–208 (DOI 10.1002/jgt.70029), so it has passed peer review by experts in the field — enough for 'resolved' status if the result had settled the whole problem, but since R(5,5)'s exact value remains open (only the range narrowed, from 43–48 to 43–46), the correct code is 'partial' with direction 'confirmed' (the bound moved in the expected/conjectured direction, no violation of expectation). The current Wikipedia article on Ramsey's theorem confirms this is the state of the art: 'it is known to lie between 43 (Geoffrey Exoo (1989)) and 46 (Angeltveit and McKay (2024)).' Separately, and NOT folded into the status/date above, I found a closely related but distinct result: Nagda, Raghavan and Thakurta (Google DeepMind), 'Reinforced Generation of Combinatorial Structures: Ramsey Numbers' (arXiv:2603.09172, submitted 2026-03-10), used AlphaEvolve — described by the authors as 'an LLM-based code mutation agent' that 'uses LLMs...to iteratively evolve code-snippets to generate better lower bounds' — to improve lower bounds on nine classical Ramsey numbers: R(3,13), R(3,18), R(4,13), R(4,14), R(4,15), R(4,16), R(4,18), R(4,19), R(4,20). This is squarely an AI-generated result on 'the values of the Ramsey numbers' in general (this bullet's broader statement covers all Ramsey numbers, with R(5,5) singled out as 'particularly' notable), but it does not touch R(5,5) or any case/restriction of R(5,5) specifically — it is a related result on different index pairs, not a case of the R(5,5) sub-problem, and is still an unreviewed 'working paper' (their own label) with no independent verification of the lower-bound constructions described in the text I read (only that the graphs were 'made public on Github'). Because the specific named quantity in this bullet is R(5,5), and the AlphaEvolve work does not change that number, I have not made it the decisive event, but it is highly relevant context for the general Ramsey-numbers problem this bullet also names.
competing_reading: If the bullet is read at its broadest — 'the values of the Ramsey numbers' as a whole, with R(5,5) as merely the illustrative example rather than the exclusive target — then the AlphaEvolve result (arXiv:2603.09172, 2026-03-10) is itself a qualifying 'case settled' (nine Ramsey-number lower bounds moved) and would make ai_role 'generated' or 'bound' for at least part of this bullet's scope, since the authors' own account is that AlphaEvolve produced the constructions/search algorithms that yielded the new bounds. Under that reading, this record would need two co-existing events: R(5,5)≤46 (no AI) and the AlphaEvolve lower-bound improvements (AI-generated/bound, still unreviewed preprint). I judged the narrower reading — that 'particularly R(5,5)' makes R(5,5) the operative target of this specific bullet, since it is the only value actually named — to be the better fit, consistent with treating other-index Ramsey numbers as a related/different problem rather than a case of 'the R(5,5) problem.' A different annotator could reasonably weight the AlphaEvolve preprint as the more AI-relevant event for this bullet given its 'values of the Ramsey numbers' framing.
what_would_settle_it: Clarification of whether this bullet's denominator is 'the value of R(5,5) alone' or 'the values of Ramsey numbers generally, exemplified by R(5,5)' would settle whether the AlphaEvolve preprint counts as a qualifying event here. Separately, peer review or independent computational verification of the AlphaEvolve lower-bound constructions (currently just a working paper with GitHub-posted graphs) would move that result from 'claimed'-type evidence to something more solid, though it would still not change the classification of this specific R(5,5) record.
